title: Theory & Research — An Overview

pts: Second language acquisition theory offers several major, genuinely competing accounts of how learning happens.
This series has drawn on many of these (Krashen, Long, Skehan) without fully unpacking their disagreements — this tier does.
Understanding the debates, not just individual findings, is what distinguishes theoretical literacy from technique collection.

v: Trainee teachers, teachers or DIET faculty
Six activity cards from earlier units

items: Prepare six cards describing familiar activities: an extensive reading slot (Unit 31), an information-gap task (Unit 30), a dictogloss, a grammar drill, a scaffolded picture-talk (Unit 15) and a corpus collocation list (Unit 58).
Draw four columns on the board: Input, Interaction, Output and Usage (frequency).
Groups place each card under the theory that best justifies it, with one sentence of reason.
Where groups disagree, ask each side what its theory predicts. Unit 77 examines the theories in full.
In an in-service programme, participants bring one activity from their own lessons instead.
Support: a one-line summary of each theory on the board.
Challenge: name one theory that would predict each activity to be of little value.

blocks.x: A discussion at a DIET workshop (written for this book):

lines: A: The drill fits nowhere. Krashen would call it learning, not acquisition.
B: A usage-based view might like it. Repetition builds frequency.
A: Only if the sentences mean something.
B: So the theory changes how we design the drill, not just whether we use it.

blocks.x: Each activity carries a hidden theory. Making it explicit is the first step towards judging it.

body: Purpose: to show that familiar activities rest on different theories. Content: four labelled columns (Input, Interaction, Output, Usage) with activity cards under them; two cards straddle columns with dotted lines. Style: clean table, labels as well as colours. Board version: a four-column table with activity names.

items: Padlet (free plan, limited number of boards) with a column layout.

blocks.x: Paper cards sorted into four chalked columns.

pts: English exists today as a plural, global phenomenon with legitimate national and regional varieties, not one standard with 'errors' elsewhere.
This formalises the critical-language-awareness thread from Tier III into a full descriptive and theoretical framework.
This has direct, practical implications for what 'correct' English actually means in a global teaching context.

v: Six short audio clips or written extracts from different varieties

items: Play six short clips of proficient English speakers, for example from India, Nigeria, Singapore, Scotland and the United States, and one Brazilian and German speaker talking together.
Participants guess where each speaker is from and note one clue.
Ask: which speakers are using ‘correct’ English? Collect answers without comment.
Introduce legitimate varieties and English as a lingua franca, then ask the question again and note how answers change.
With learners, compare an Indian newspaper editorial, a Nigerian story extract and a British news report.
Support: a list of countries to choose from.
Challenge: identify one feature regular in one variety but marked in another.

lines: Indian English: prepone; cousin-brother; I am having two sisters.
Singapore English: discourse particles such as lah in informal speech.
T: Is ‘prepone’ an error?
S1: It is not in my old dictionary.
S2: But everyone in my office understands it.
T: So who decides?

blocks.x: The descriptive position developed in Units 74 and 78 is that established varieties are rule-governed systems, not collections of mistakes (Kachru 1985).

body: Purpose: to show English as plural. Content: a world map with speech bubbles over India, Nigeria, Singapore, the United Kingdom and the United States, each with one characteristic expression. Style: clean map, no flags. Board version: a rough world outline with labelled bubbles.

items: Speech Accent Archive (free, George Mason University) for one paragraph read by speakers of many backgrounds.

blocks.x: The teacher reads written extracts aloud.

pts: Teachers' often-implicit beliefs about language and learning shape practice as powerfully as formal training does.
This extends Tier III's brief introduction (Unit 72) into the full research field studying this phenomenon.
Understanding your own cognition is itself a form of the reflective expertise this series has built toward.

items: Read a belief statement, for example Errors should be corrected immediately.
Participants stand along a line from ‘strongly agree’ to ‘strongly disagree’ (or, on fixed benches, hold up one to five fingers).
Ask two people from opposite ends to explain their positions.
Ask: Does what you do in class match where you are standing? Participants note one gap between belief and practice. Unit 79 returns to this gap.
Use an anonymous poll where open disagreement with seniors is uncomfortable.
Support: a sentence frame, I stand here because in my class….
Challenge: trace one belief to its origin, for example your own schooling.

lines: A: I strongly agree. If you don’t correct at once, the error becomes permanent.
B: My learners stop speaking if I correct everything.
T: And this week, how often did you correct at once?
A: Almost always. It is how I was taught.

blocks.x: That last remark describes what Lortie (1975) called the apprenticeship of observation: beliefs about teaching formed during years of watching teachers as a pupil.

body: Purpose: to introduce teacher cognition. Content: an iceberg; above water, classroom actions (correcting, explaining, grouping); below, beliefs, memories of school and assumptions. Style: calm blues. Board version: a triangle with a waterline and labels.

items: Mentimeter (free plan) or Google Forms (free) for an anonymous agreement scale.

blocks.x: Slips of paper placed in a box.

body: When principals and junior teachers are in the same session, an anonymous vote gives more honest results than a public line-up. Use the public version once the group trusts each other.

pts: Materials design (Tier III, Unit 69) rests on research findings about grading, authenticity, and task design worth examining directly.
This tier grounds that practical craft in its underlying evidence base.
Understanding the research strengthens, rather than replaces, the practical materials-writing skill already built.

blocks.x: Why is this page designed like this?

v: One coursebook unit in current use

items: For each activity in the unit, ask: What input does it give? What does it ask learners to do with meaning? What must they produce?
Mark any activity whose design no learning principle explains.
Discuss whether each choice is driven by research, tradition, examination format or page space.
Note one change you would make and the evidence you would cite. Unit 80 develops a full framework.
Compare an older and a newer textbook for the same class.
Support: the three questions as a printed grid.
Challenge: rewrite one activity to match a principle better.

blocks.x: Notes on a typical reading lesson (written for this book):

lines: Pre-reading: Answer in one word. Little activation of ideas or feeling.
Post-reading: ten factual questions; one grammar exercise unconnected to the text.
Missing: engagement before reading; meaningful output that uses the text.

blocks.x: Tomlinson (2011) argues that materials should achieve impact, engage learners affectively and cognitively, and provide opportunities for communicative use. Principles like these move evaluation from ‘I like it’ to reasons that can be shared.

body: Purpose: to link design choices to principles. Content: a coursebook double page with arrows from activities to labels ‘input’, ‘engagement’, ‘output’ and ‘no clear principle’. Style: annotated sketch. Board version: boxes with arrows and labels.

items: DIKSHA (free, Government of India) for digital state and NCERT textbooks.

blocks.x: A photocopied unit annotated in pencil.

points.sub: How the field knows what it knows
pts: Understanding how ELT research is actually conducted — its methods, strengths, and limitations — supports critical, informed reading of the field.
This extends Tier III's action-research introduction (Unit 67) into the broader landscape of formal research methodology.
This is genuinely useful for evaluating claims — including many made throughout this very series.

v: Four short research claims from different sources

items: Give groups four claims, for example from a newspaper, a coursebook introduction, a workshop handout and a research summary.
For each, groups ask: Who was studied? How many? For how long? What was measured? What else could explain the result?
Groups rate each claim as strong, moderate or weak evidence for their own classroom.
Choose one claim to test through action research (Unit 67). Unit 81 treats research methods fully.
Apply the same questions to claims made in this book.
Support: a glossary of sample, control group and variable.
Challenge: sketch a small study to test one claim in a DIET partner school.

lines: Claim: Learners who use this app for ten minutes a day improve their vocabulary by 40%. Compared with what? Measured how? Who funded it?
T: So do we reject the claim?
S1: Not reject. Ask for the study.
S2: And try it with one section and compare.

blocks.x: Dörnyei (2007) sets out the strengths and limits of quantitative, qualitative and mixed methods. Asking ‘how do they know?’ is the most useful research habit a teacher can have.

body: Purpose: to give a portable critical-reading routine. Content: a magnifying glass over a headline, surrounded by five questions. Style: clear infographic. Board version: a box with five arrows.

items: Google Scholar (free) and ERIC (free, US Department of Education) for finding original studies.

blocks.x: The five questions on a card inside the teaching journal.

pts: Cognitive linguistics offers a distinct account of how grammar and meaning are mentally organised, with real pedagogical implications.
This provides an alternative, complementary lens to Chomskyan Universal Grammar, referenced since Unit 6.
This is one of several theoretical frameworks worth understanding, not a single replacement for the others.

items: Draw a central meaning for over: a bird flying above and across a house.
Show extended uses: jump over the wall, the class is over, think it over, over 100 people.
Pairs link each use to the central picture and explain the connection.
Compare how Kannada, Hindi or Tamil expresses the same ideas, then add two new examples with pictures.
Use the same approach for phrasal verbs with up.
Support: a picture for each sentence to match.
Challenge: group corpus examples (Unit 58) by meaning.

lines: The plane flew over the city. (above and across)
The class is over. (across to the end: completion)
S1: In Hindi we say ‘khatam’. It is a different word.
T: Yes. English uses the picture of crossing to the end; Hindi uses a word for finishing. Both make sense.

blocks.x: Cognitive linguistics holds that meanings are organized around central images and extended by metaphor, rather than being lists of unrelated uses (Littlemore 2009). Unit 82 examines it as an alternative to the Chomskyan view introduced in Unit 6.

body: Purpose: to show a polysemy network. Content: an arc over a house labelled ‘over’, with spokes to small pictures for each extended use. Style: friendly line drawing. Board version: an arc, a box and four spokes.

items: Canva for Education (free for teachers) for picture networks.

pts: Sociocultural theory frames learning as fundamentally social and mediated, not purely individual cognitive processing.
This provides the deeper theoretical grounding for cooperative learning (Tier II, Unit 34) and scaffolding (Tier I, Unit 15).
The Zone of Proximal Development concept underlies much of this series' scaffolding guidance, made explicit here.

v: A transcript of a teacher helping a learner

items: Show a transcript of a teacher helping a learner describe a picture.
Trainees label each teacher move: hinting, simplifying, modelling or giving the answer.
Ask: did the help decrease as the learner became more able? Where could the teacher have waited?
Introduce the zone of proximal development (Vygotsky 1978), and plan a sequence from implicit to explicit help. Unit 83 develops sociocultural theory fully.
Trainees record themselves helping one learner and analyse their moves.
Support: a completed example sheet.
Challenge: compare teacher scaffolding with peer scaffolding in cooperative groups (Unit 34).

lines: S1: Yesterday I… go… to market.
T: Yesterday?
S1: Yesterday I goed…
T: Not goed. Think: yesterday I…
S1: Went! Yesterday I went to the market.

blocks.x: The teacher gave the least help that worked. Aljaafreh and Lantolf (1994) described feedback of this kind as graduated and contingent: offered as needed and withdrawn when not.

body: Purpose: to show scaffolding and fading. Content: a building in three stages, with scaffolding dense, then lighter, then gone; a learner stands on the finished roof. Style: simple, warm. Board version: three rectangles with fewer lines around each.

items: Audacity (free, open source) or a phone recorder for short exchanges.

blocks.x: A transcript written from memory straight after the lesson.

body: The metaphor of scaffolding is not Vygotsky’s own. It was introduced by David Wood, Jerome Bruner and Gail Ross (1976) in a study of adults tutoring young children, and was later linked with the zone of proximal development.

points.h: AI and the Future of ELT
pts: Artificial intelligence is already reshaping language learning tools, assessment, and teacher workflows in real time.
This tier addresses both the genuine opportunities and the real, unresolved questions this shift raises.
This closes the series looking forward, not just backward at established theory.

v: One device with an AI chatbot, or printed outputs; a short learner text

items: Ask a chatbot to correct a short learner paragraph, write a five-question reading quiz and explain the present perfect for Class 8.
Groups ask of each output: Is it accurate? Suitable for our learners? What does it miss? Does it treat Indian English as error?
Rate each job ‘use’, ‘use with editing’ or ‘do not use’.
Draft three rules on AI use for your school or DIET. Unit 84 treats AI in ELT, and Unit 99 its ethics in assessment.
Without a device, the facilitator brings printed outputs.
Support: an evaluation grid.
Challenge: run one prompt twice and discuss what varying answers mean for assessment.

lines: A: It changed ‘I am having two sisters’ to ‘I have two sisters’, but did not say the first is common in Indian English.
B: And it rewrote the whole paragraph. The learner’s voice is gone.
Draft rule: Teachers check every AI-generated quiz before use.
Draft rule: Learners may use AI feedback on a draft but submit their own revision, noting what they changed.

blocks.x: Kohnke, Moorhouse and Zou (2023) discuss both the potential and the risks of chatbots in language teaching. The field moves quickly, so any rule should be reviewed each year.

body: Purpose: to show AI as promising and unresolved. Content: a balance; one pan holds ‘instant feedback’, ‘materials drafts’, ‘practice partner’; the other ‘accuracy’, ‘bias’, ‘privacy’, ‘learner effort’. Style: neutral. Board version: a T-chart.

items: ChatGPT (free and paid tiers), Microsoft Copilot (free) and Google Gemini (free and paid tiers). Check age limits and data policies before any learner use. [VERIFY current age and privacy terms]

blocks.x: Printed AI outputs evaluated in groups.

body: Choose the field in this unit you know least about. Before reading its full unit, write three things you believe about it. Afterwards, mark which beliefs changed, which held, and which you now want to test in your own classroom.

dek: Unit 76 of 100: the final tier opens. Where Tier III built expert practice, Tier IV turns to the underlying science, scholarship, and open questions that ground it.

aims.x: This unit opens Part IV. Parts I to III built a working practice: planning, teaching, integrating skills, assessing and designing. Part IV asks why any of it should work. Every technique in this book rests on some theory of how languages are learned, what English is and how teachers think. This unit is a map of that ground: each point introduces one field and names the later unit that treats it in full. The activities are mainly teacher-education and classroom-research tasks for experienced teachers, trainee teachers and DIET faculty.
By the end of this unit you should be able to:

items: explain why theoretical literacy differs from collecting techniques;
name the main competing accounts of second language acquisition;
describe English as a plural, global language and say what this means for ‘correctness’;
recognize teacher cognition as a field that studies your own beliefs;
link materials-design choices to their research base;
read a research claim critically, asking how it was produced;
contrast cognitive linguistic and sociocultural lenses on learning;
identify the opportunities and open questions that artificial intelligence brings to ELT.

why: Why this matters. Every technique in this series rests on some theory of how language is learned. Tier IV makes those theories explicit, alongside their genuine, ongoing debates.

background.x: Language teaching has always borrowed its ideas: grammar-translation from the teaching of Latin, audiolingualism from behaviourist psychology, communicative teaching from sociolinguistics. The field of second language acquisition (SLA), which grew from the 1970s, tried to put teaching on a firmer empirical footing by studying how learners actually develop. It produced not one answer but several strong, competing accounts (Mitchell, Myles and Marsden 2019). A teacher who knows only techniques can follow a method; a teacher who knows the debates can judge when a technique fits.

Confident claims are everywhere: in coursebook blurbs, workshop slides and policy circulars. Theoretical literacy includes knowing how research is done, what an experiment can and cannot show, and why a case study may not generalize (Dörnyei 2007). It also includes knowing that teachers’ own beliefs filter everything they read (Borg 2003). Part IV therefore studies both the learner’s mind and the teacher’s.

India gives this part particular weight. It is one of the largest English-using societies in the world, with its own established variety, and one of the most multilingual. N. S. Prabhu’s Communicational Teaching Project in Bangalore schools contributed to international theory rather than merely applying it (Prabhu 1987). NEP 2020 asks teachers to be reflective professionals who value home languages, and NCF 2023 grounds its language approach in research on multilingualism and learning (Ministry of Human Resource Development 2020; NCERT 2023). Theory rarely tells a teacher what to do on Monday morning, but it makes choices explicit and gives reasons that can be discussed with colleagues, heads and parents.

items: Theory mapping. A table linking six of your own activities to the theories that justify them.
Critical reading. A short evaluation of one published claim using the five questions of point 5.
Belief statement. Three beliefs about learning, each with its origin and a note on whether practice matches it.
AI policy draft. Three to five rules on AI use for a school or DIET, each with a reason.
Which theory of learning does your teaching most often assume, even unnamed?
How do you usually respond to an Indian English expression in class?
Which of your beliefs about teaching came from your own schooling?
When did you last change a practice because of evidence rather than instruction?
How do you decide whether a new claim about teaching deserves your time?
What would you want to know about an AI tool before learners use it?

terms.def: Lortie’s (1975) term for the many hours future teachers spend watching their own teachers as pupils, which shapes their beliefs about teaching before any training begins.
An approach to language that sees it as grounded in general human cognition and experience, and studies meaning through categories, metaphor and constructions.

The systematic judgement of the value of learning materials against explicit criteria, before, during or after use; an evaluation framework makes those criteria clear and helps teachers compare coursebooks consistently.

The procedures used to collect and analyse evidence, such as experiments, surveys, interviews, observation and case studies. Understanding their strengths and limits helps teachers judge what a study can and cannot show about classrooms.

Temporary support that helps learners do what they could not yet do alone, gradually withdrawn as competence grows (Wood, Bruner and Ross 1976). Examples include sentence frames, modelling, visual prompts and guiding questions.

The study of how people learn languages other than their first, and the processes involved. The acronym SLA refers both to the process and to the research field, which informs many teaching decisions.
What teachers know, believe and think, and how this relates to what they do in the classroom (Borg 2003). It is shaped by schooling, training, experience and context.
The ability to understand and critically evaluate theories and research claims in language teaching, including how research is done and what it can show. It differs from simply collecting techniques.

The varieties of English used around the world, such as Indian, Nigerian and Singaporean English, each seen as legitimate with its own norms. The concept is closely associated with Kachru’s Three Circles model.

The gap between what a learner can do alone and what they can do with support from a teacher or more capable peer (Vygotsky 1978). Teaching aimed within this zone, with scaffolding, promotes development.
